summary.title: Freeze-Float System for High-throughput Measurement of Ice Nucleation
summary.executive_summary: This paper presents the development of a high-throughput screening implementation of the freeze-float selection platform for measuring ice nucleation. The primary objective is to expand the system's throughput and accuracy by automating droplet generation and improving temperature uniformity. The authors address the limitations of their previous proof-of-concept system, which suffered from low thermal conductivity in silicone oil and non-uniform cooling across multiple cuvettes. To overcome these challenges, they introduced the Biomek 3000 robotic liquid handling system for automated, uniform droplet generation in 96-well plates, achieving a polydispersity of 9.2%. They also implemented the Asymptote VIA controlled-rate freezer to ensure homogeneous cooling, significantly reducing well-to-well variability compared to generic freezers. The study demonstrates that the new system can process up to 1920 droplets simultaneously, increasing throughput by a factor of 38. Validation experiments using Snomax as an ice nucleating agent showed improved differentiation accuracy and lower dispersion in freezing temperatures. The automated system successfully identified ice-nucleating activity with high precision, although challenges regarding droplet stability during transport due to static electricity were noted. The integration of automated dispensing and controlled cooling represents a significant advancement in the efficiency and reliability of ice nucleation assays, facilitating large-scale screening of ice-nucleating entities.

claims.description: The automated system significantly increases throughput and accuracy of ice nucleation measurements.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper presents the development of a high-throughput screening implementation of the freeze-float selection platform for measuring ice nucleation. The primary objective is to expand the system's throughput and accuracy by automating droplet generation and improving temperature uniformity. The authors address the limitations of their previous proof-of-concept system, which suffered from low thermal conductivity in silicone oil and non-uniform cooling across multiple cuvettes. To overcome these challenges, they introduced the Biomek 3000 robotic liquid handling system for automated, uniform droplet generation in 96-well plates, achieving a polydispersity of 9.2%. They also implemented the Asymptote VIA controlled-rate freezer to ensure homogeneous cooling, significantly reducing well-to-well variability compared to generic freezers. The study demonstrates that the new system can process up to 1920 droplets simultaneously, increasing throughput by a factor of 38. Validation experiments using Snomax as an ice nucleating agent showed improved differentiation accuracy and lower dispersion in freezing temperatures. The automated system successfully identified ice-nucleating activity with high precision, although challenges regarding droplet stability during transport due to static electricity were noted. The integration of automated dispensing and controlled cooling represents a significant advancement in the efficiency and reliability of ice nucleation assays, facilitating large-scale screening of ice-nucleating entities.

Research Context
Previous proof-of-concept systems used 1 cm2 cuvettes with limited throughput. Low thermal conductivity of silicone oil prevented larger container footprints. Setting up multiple cuvettes in parallel resulted in non-uniform temperature distributions. High-throughput screening (HTS) in multi-well plates is well-established for drug discovery. Droplet-based assays offer chemical compartmentalization to avoid cross-contamination. Polydispersity in droplet size directly influences freezing temperature accuracy. Microfluidics can produce uniform droplets but interfacing with HTS plates is non-trivial.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The goal is to expand the system to higher throughput and accuracy. The system aims to increase screening efficiency with fewer manipulation steps. Increased sample size is hypothesized to improve measurement accuracy. Incorporating a controlled-rate freezer is expected to improve temperature uniformity. Droplet freezing is hypothesized to be a random nucleation process. Stochastic freezing behavior causes spread in freezing temperatures among identical droplets. Expanding assay vessel size increases throughput by a factor of 38.

Methodological Details
The study used a 96 deep well plate compatible with Biomek 3000. Silicone oil with 1% surfactant and HFE-7500 cushion layer were used. 30 x 1 µL droplets were dispensed into the silicone oil layer. The Biomek 3000 generated 40 uniform droplets in 96 wells in ~15 minutes. Droplet dispersity was assessed using fluorescein dye and image analysis. Matlab automated circle detection program measured droplet diameters. Polydispersity of 60 droplets was calculated as 9.2%. An Auto-set Ion Pump was used to remove static electricity. Validation used 30 aqueous droplets with 1 mg/mL Snomax. Kolmogorov-Smirnov test compared freezing temperature distributions of two samples. The Asymptote VIA freezer accommodated up to 48 x 1 mL cryovials. Each cryovial contained 20 Snomax droplets and 20 water droplets.

Procedures And Architectures
Automated droplet generation was performed using the Biomek 3000 robotic system. Droplets were generated at a rate of 1 droplet per 2 seconds. HFE-7500 was placed at the bottom to prevent droplet destabilization. Static electricity was managed using an ion pump and wet filter paper. The Asymptote VIA freezer provided constant rate cooling down to -0.5 °C/min. A custom-made glass lid enabled automated image recording by a digital camera. Freezing temperatures were recorded using a generic digital camera. Python script KStest.ipynb was used for statistical comparison of distributions. The system was tested with linear cooling at -0.25 °C/min.

Key Results
The Biomek 3000 generated up to ~3800 droplets at once. Droplet polydispersity was measured at 9.2%. Expected dispersion in nucleation temperature was no more than ±0.09 °C. INA droplets froze at -7.1 ±0.59 °C in the Asymptote freezer. Non-INA droplets did not freeze until -12.3 °C. Controlled cooling provided better detection than commodity freezers (-7.5 ±0.97 °C). Well-to-well variability in 96 deep well system had p = 0.31. Asymptote freezer showed less well-to-well difference with p = 0.83. Standard deviation in Asymptote freezer was 0.73 compared to 1.6 in 96-well. Overall dispersion was 36% lower in the Asymptote freezer.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
Automated dispensing ensures uniform droplet volume, critical for quantitative detection. Controlled-rate cooling improves temperature uniformity across multiple wells. The system enables high-throughput screening of ice-nucleating entities. Stochastic nature of nucleation requires large sample sizes for reliable measurement. The method bridges microfluidic precision with HTS scalability.

Contradictions And Limitations
Droplet stability was insufficient during transport due to static electricity. Combining droplet generation and transport was not successful. 96-well plates showed significant thermal gradients despite linear cooling. Mean freezing time differed between cells in 96-well plates.

Claims
The automated system significantly increases throughput and accuracy of ice nucleation measurements. Throughput increased by a factor of 38. Dispersion was 36% lower in controlled freezer. Transport issues limited full automation integration. Enables large-scale screening of ice nucleators.

Data And Code Availability
Source code for droplet dispersion analysis is provided as Source Code S1. Python script for statistical testing is provided as Source Code S3.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Comparison between generic freezer and Asymptote freezer showed improved uniformity. Linear cooling reduced thermal gradient compared to constant temperature cooling.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows automated droplet generation and dispersity analysis. Figure 2 shows freeze-float validation with Snomax. Figure 3 shows thermal gradient in 96-well plate. Figure 4 shows freezing temperatures in Asymptote freezer. Figure 5 shows well-to-well variability in Asymptote freezer. Figure 6 compares dispersion between systems.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is a high-throughput freeze-float system with automated droplet generation. 2. The strongest evidence is the 36% reduction in dispersion using controlled-rate cooling. 3. The future path involves overcoming transport stability issues for full automation.
